v: A half-cooked story rescued by Nani’s terrific raw performance, striking cinematography and some genuinely powerful action — ultimately a solid one-time watch.
e: Dasara had the ingredients for a stronger village political drama, but the writing shifts focus and never feels fully cooked. What keeps it engaging is Nani stepping convincingly into a raw mass role, supported by terrific cinematography, strong action staging and an effective BGM.
body:
For me, Dasara is an average-to-good movie that is worth watching mainly for the performances of its lead cast and the raw cinematography.

Content-wise, the film had the potential to become a strong political drama set in a 1990s village.

But somewhere along the way, the writing seems eager to avoid obvious comparisons with Rangasthalam and shifts more of its focus towards the love-versus-lust angle.

Because of that, the core story feels a little half-cooked to me.

What the film lacks in writing depth, it tries to compensate for through some terrific visuals and raw action sequences.

The songs are only average for me, but the BGM works very well and lifts both the action and emotional scenes.

The biggest strength, without doubt, is Nani.

This is the first time I really saw him embrace such a raw, massy character. We can conveniently ignore a couple of earlier experiments in that zone 😜

Because audiences are so used to seeing Nani in boy-next-door roles, it takes a little time to sync with his rugged look and Telangana accent.

But once that adjustment happens, his performance is easily the most memorable part of the movie and once again proves what an excellent actor he is.

Overall, Dasara is a one-time watch for me — technically impressive and strongly performed, but with a story that could have gone much deeper.

v: A proper commercial entertainer carried by Vishwak Sen — fun first half, well-placed twists, terrific second-character energy and a BGM that knows exactly when to kick in.
e: Das Ki Dhamki works because Vishwak Sen commits completely to the commercial format while still giving himself room to perform. The first half is entertaining, the twists keep the screenplay moving, and his second role plus Leon James’ BGM give the film its strongest moments.
body:
I was never a big fan of Vishwak Sen initially, and I absolutely hated Falaknuma Das for its slow and overly realistic treatment 😅

But his performances in the films that followed gradually started grabbing my attention.

So I was genuinely curious to see how Das Ki Dhamki would turn out, especially because this was Vishwak attempting a full-length commercial entertainer in a much bigger way.

Content-wise, it is a proper commercial plot.

The first half is mostly focused on entertainment, songs and setting up the interval block.

Then comes the interval twist, followed by another major turn in the second half.

The structure itself is familiar, but Vishwak Sen’s direction and performance add considerable energy to it.

Acting-wise, he is at his casual best through most of the first half.

But it is the second character that really gives him room to show his acting range — and man, he simply nails it.

Some viewers may find portions of that performance a little overboard, but within this film’s commercial tone it worked for me.

Nivetha Pethuraj, on the other hand, felt slightly over-the-top in a few places, though that may also be because of the way her character was written.

The rest of the supporting cast does its job comfortably.

Special mention to Leon James’ BGM, which gives the action and suspense portions a very effective lift 🙏

Overall, Das Ki Dhamki is a good, entertaining watch and a film where Vishwak Sen’s confidence as both actor and filmmaker is clearly visible.

v: A familiar family-drama theme transformed into a MUST WATCH by powerhouse performances — Prakash Raj is superb, but Brahmanandam revealing this emotional side is unforgettable 🙏
e: Ranga Maarthaanda may tell a broadly familiar story about ageing parents and changing family relationships, but the stage-artist perspective gives it added depth. Prakash Raj is predictably excellent, while Brahmanandam delivers the revelation of the film with a deeply emotional performance that completely changes how we see him.
body:
A few years before Ranga Maarthaanda, I first came across the teaser of the Marathi film Natsamrat, starring the great Nana Patekar and directed by Mahesh Manjrekar.

It immediately grabbed my attention because both the actor and director were people I admired a lot.

I never managed to watch the original because of the language barrier, but I knew it had been critically acclaimed.

Years later, when I heard Krishna Vamsi was remaking the same story in Telugu with Prakash Raj, I became equally excited.

Another director and actor I admire were adapting a movie I had always wanted to experience — so this was one film I was determined to watch on the big screen irrespective of the talk 😊

At its core, the story travels through territory we have seen in films such as Baghban and several other family dramas: ageing parents, changing priorities, career-driven children and the emotional distance that can grow inside a family.

So the basic idea itself is not new.

What makes Ranga Maarthaanda more interesting is the way it integrates the life and identity of a stage artist into that familiar family conflict.

We already know how brilliant Prakash Raj can be, and this film simply reminds us why he is considered one of our finest actors.

But the real show-stealer for me is Brahmanandam.

Most of us grew up watching his comedy. His expressions became part of our everyday humour and, years later, our meme culture.

Here, the same man makes us cry.

His emotional performance is outstanding and reminds us that somewhere along the way we became so used to his comedy that we forgot what a complete actor he actually is 🙏🙏

I genuinely hope roles like this open another phase in his career.

Shivathmika is another pleasant surprise. Surrounded by such experienced performers, she still manages to make her presence felt.

Rahul Sipligunj and Anasuya also leave an impression in their respective roles.

Ilaiyaraaja’s music and BGM are soothing, the lyrics carry depth, and several dialogues have a strong philosophical quality.

What might otherwise have been merely a good watch built around a familiar theme becomes a MUST WATCH for me because of Brahmanandam and Prakash Raj.

v: A modest film that saves its best for the final 30 minutes — once the real emotion lands, Rohini and Ashish Vidyarthi turn a simple story into a genuine MUST WATCH ❤️
e: Writer Padmabhushan moves through a pleasant but fairly average middle stretch before revealing the emotional idea that gives the film its identity. The final thirty minutes are the heart of the movie, with Rohini and Ashish Vidyarthi emerging as the true show-stealers alongside an effortless Suhas.
body:
I still can’t believe I missed Writer Padmabhushan on the big screen 😞

For its core emotion alone, this is a MUST WATCH.

The movie starts on a good note, then moves through a fairly average stretch with bits of entertainment here and there.

And then the final thirty minutes arrive.

That section is the heart of the film and completely changes the overall experience.

Without that emotional payoff, Writer Padmabhushan might have remained an average feel-good movie for me.

With it, the story suddenly finds a much deeper purpose.

Suhas makes the lead role look effortless — by this point, this kind of natural performance almost feels like a cakewalk for him.

But the real show-stealers are Rohini and Ashish Vidyarthi 🙏🙏🙏

Their performances give the final portions the emotional weight the story needs.

I do feel the film could have been mounted and crafted even better, because the central emotion deserved the strongest possible presentation.

Budget limitations may have led to some compromises.

Still, the scenes and screenplay retain a natural quality, and when the film finally reveals what it really wants to say, the emotion lands beautifully.

That final stretch is what stayed with me — and it is the reason Writer Padmabhushan rises well above its otherwise simple packaging.
